item.title: 2027: Opposition’s battle for space
item.description: Within a span of one week, opposition political parties in Nigeria have experienced various challenges in their bid to contest in the 2027 general elections. From the bids for the presidency to governorship, national assembly and state assembly seats, opposition candidates have not been finding it easy to campaign as they wish as they are faced with various forms of harassment, suppression and intimidation. Weekend Trust reports that 31 states in the country are under the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) while two of the remaining five opposition governors have been included in the presidential campaign council of the party. Our correspondents recall that within the week, the convoy of the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) was attacked in Cross Rivers State, while the bid by the African Democratic Congress (ADC) to hold a rally in Sokoto met with stiff opposition and in Edo and Plateau States, the billboards of major opposition candidates were pulled down. On Thursday, a Federal High Court sitting in Abuja also nullified all the processes of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) that led to the emergence of former Vice President Atiku Abubakar as the party’s candidate for the 2027 election. Justice Peter Lifu, in a judgement, nullified the emergence of the former Senate President, David Mark, Rauf Aregbesola and others as national officers of the ADC. The judge held that the nominations of candidates for the 2027 general elections were cancelled on account of emerging from an “illegal and unlawful leadership.” In the same day, the presidential campaign convoy of the ADC was reportedly attacked in Kebbi State, as the candidate, Atiku, moved through Kebbi on campaign engagements on Thursday. According to reports from the campaign team, thugs blocked the convoy and pelted vehicles with stones. These developments, according to political observers, represent a systematic weakening of opposition parties and raise concerns over Nigeria’s democracy. Due to the frequency in occurrence, opposition figures and civil society organisations have accused the ruling party, APC, of utilizing state-backed coercion, judicial manipulation, and targeted inducements to systematically dismantle counter-balancing political structures across the country. Critics warn that by neutralising alternative political platforms ahead of upcoming electoral cycles, the APC-led administration is actively eroding the essential checks and balances required for democratic accountability. Efforts to get the ruling party (APC) at the national level to respond to the allegations proved abortive as the National Publicity Secretary of the party, Felix Morka, did not respond to phone calls or WhatsApp messages sent to him. item.title: Habiba: The woman behind ‘Jaiz Bank’s N100m investment scheme’
item.description: The protest over the N104 million Mudarabah investment and the alleged withdrawal from customers’ accounts at Jaiz Bank, Jos, on Monday, has raised questions with many asking how such could have occurred. One staff member of the bank, Habiba Abdulrahman, is at the centre of the scandal. Mrs Abdulrahman, 35, is a resident of Muhammadu Wada Street, Jos North Local Government Area of Plateau State. She had her primary education at Women Association Primary School, Jos. Thereafter, she proceeded to Federal Government Girls’ College, Bauchi. In 2009, she gained admission into the Abubakar Tafawa Balewa University (ATBU), Bauchi, where she read Environmental Management Technology. She taught at Esteem Secondary School. And between 2018 and 2019, she was employed by Jaiz Bank as a contract customer service officer and subsequently rose to the position of Operations Head (Backup), with the primary duty of approving withdrawals and transfers initiated by tellers in the bank. Weekend Trust gathered that Habiba was sacked by the bank in January 2026, after the irregularities were detected. On Monday this week, affected customers who found their accounts emptied by the alleged sacked staff staged a protest in front of the bank in Jos, asking it to refund their money. They also called on the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) and other relevant authorities to come to their aid, adding that despite several complaints to the bank’s management, the money had not been refunded. The customers alleged that when the matter was earlier reported to the bank’s management, they were informed that the money had been transferred to several bank accounts by a staff member. The protesters insisted that the transactions were carried out within the banking hall using documents approved by the bank. The protesters at the entrance of the bank on Monday. We found fake Jaiz Bank certificates of fixed deposits, documents in Habiba’s house – Police Following a complaint to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) of the Plateau State police command by the Jaiz Bank Jos branch manager, Victoria Amidu, in January this year, the CID arrested Habiba, Weekend Trust gathered. In its findings dated June 19, 2026, obtained by Weekend Trust from the lawyer of one of the victims, N. A. Idoko, the CID accused Habiba of conspiracy, cheating and fraud during her transactions with the affected customers. The police also accused Habiba of conniving with her husband, Manir Murtala, 44, and her younger sister, Zainab Abdulrahman, 21, whose accounts were allegedly used to transfer customers’ money into theirs. According to the report, after a search warrant was conducted in the house and premises of the suspects, some relevant Jaiz Bank documents were recovered from her possession. item.title: The night of January 15, 1966 – General Paul Tarfa
item.description: General Paul Chabiri Tarfa joined the Nigerian Army as a cadet in 1962 and remained there until 1988, serving for 26 years. In that span of time he held many positions – Assistant Adjutant General, Provost Marshal, Commandant of the Nigerian Defence Academy. He also served as the governor of the old Oyo State in 1978. After retirement, he served as the managing director of the Nigerian Railways and also had a brief assignment to reorganise the Nigerian Customs. At 85, he is still busy as the chairman of the North-East Development Commission. He shared his experiences with Weekend Trust. I would like to start with your home, Garkida, which I think is a well-known centre for missionary and western education. Do you think the fact that you were born there has had a very huge impact on how your life turned out? Of course, Garkida is one of the old places in the North where missionaries set up and gave us good footing in education. I must say that in those days we were privileged to have been among the early people in the North, especially the North-East, to be introduced to western education. Habiba: The woman behind ‘Jaiz Bank’s N100m investment scheme’ 2027: Opposition’s battle for space That is not to say that Islamic education was not there, but surely, we were lucky to have the missionaries as far back as March 1923, to be precise. You can imagine that it is well over 100 years now. We have benefitted. We had early education and were introduced to secondary school. We had good medical care, which many of our people in the North were not privileged to have. We went from primary to secondary school, from where we had the advantage of being successfully qualified to get enrolled into the Nigerian Army. I think you went to secondary school in Yola and not Garkida, right? Well, Garkida laid the foundation before going to Yola – provincial secondary school in those days. There were only 12 in the entire North and Yola was one of them. It was from there that I had the opportunity to get into the army. You became a cadet in the army in April 1962, but it didn’t take long before you were taken to Canada, a very strange place for someone coming from this part of the world. Before going there, we were told what it would be. Even before then, in Geography in secondary school, we had known about temperate countries, hot countries and so on, of which Canada was one. So when we got to Canada, we were very well equipped and properly prepared, physically and mentally. Your career in the army took off after you returned to Canada. This was 1963? Yes. We came back in December 1963, received at Kano airport, taken to Kaduna and received by the duty officer, who at that time happened to be a man called Benjamin Adekunle. He was a captain and we were just second lieutenants. The so-called “black scorpion”? He asked: “Who among you is Paul Tarfa?” I said I was the one and he said “congratulations”. item.title: Anambra will deliver over 50% of 2027 votes to Tinubu — Soludo
item.description: By Vincent Ujumadu Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, has promised to deliver at least 50 percent of the state’s votes to President Bola Tinubu, the presidential candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC), in the 2027 general elections. Read Also: Tinubu to Nigerians: ‘I promise better future’ The governor made the declaration during the flag off of the All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) 2027 campaign at Ekwueme Square, Awka. According to him, APGA has no presidential candidate for the 2027 general election and would, therefore, adopt President Tinubu as its preferred candidate. “Today, we adopt the APC presidential candidate, Bola Ahmed Tinubu as our candidate,” he declared, noting that the president had demonstrated love and concern for the Igbo people, particularly the people of Anambra State. The governor recalled that the President had appointed several Anambra indigenes to strategic positions in Lagos State during his tenure as governor. He also recalled that APGA had adopted the presidential candidate of the ruling party in previous elections, noting that the party’s decision to support Tinubu in 2027 was a continuation of that political arrangement that had been in existence. He lamented that Anambra State recorded fewer than 5,000 votes for Tinubu in the 2023 presidential election, yet the President has continued to address some of the challenges confronting the state and the South-East region. He urged the Anambra electorate to support Tinubu in the 2027 election, arguing that doing so would give the state and the South-East a stronger opportunity to engage with the Federal Government and negotiate for their development. “We need to vote for him in order to sit with the government at the centre and negotiate for the development of the South-East and Anambra State”, he declared. item.title: Tinubu’s reforms need time to deliver, 2nd term will consolidate gains — Aguda
item.description: Oluwole Aguda is a businessman, consultant on electoral mat- ters and political affairs, and a former governorship aspirant in Kogi State, under the African Action Con- gress (AAC) in 2019. In this interview, he examines President Bola Tinubu’s reform agenda, the steps the President must take to secure electoral support in the North ahead of the 2027 general election, and the political implications of the lingering face-off between Imo State Governor Hope Uzodimma and his predecessor, Senator Rochas Okoro- cha, over the Imo West senatorial ticket. Excerpts: Given the hardship caused by fuel subsidy removal, naira devaluation and other economic policies, what tangible improvements in Nigerians’ living conditions can President Tinubu point to as justification for seeking a second term? A fair assessment requires us to examine the immediate challenges confronting the economy and the long-term benefits expected from the reforms. Nigeria’s economy was bleeding, and stopping that haemorrhage was necessary to give the country a chance of recovery. Ending fuel subsidy addressed an avenue for corruption and the unsustainable drain on public resources. NELFUND had disbursed over N300 billion to over 1.5m students across 319 tertiary institutions as at October 2026. However, I would not suggest that these developments have largely translated into improved living conditions for most Nigerians. That remains the administration’s biggest challenge. The cost of food, transportation, housing, healthcare and other essentials continues to put enormous pressure on households. Economic recovery must ultimately be measured by whether people can afford necessities, businesses can employ more workers and incomes can support a reasonable standard of living. The President’s case for another term should not rest solely on the courage to introduce reforms. It must also depend on translating them into better purchasing power, employment, productivity and social welfare. Reforms require time, but Nigerians enduring difficult adjustments must see a credible pathway to relief. How would you assess the Tinubu administration’s performance, and what justifies giving it another four years? There is intention coupled with execution across different sectoral interventions. While execution has been a challenge, progressive steps have been made. Investment in our military is important to sustaining a motivated Army, Navy and Air Force in the war against terrorism. The Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway also promises to reduce travel time and transportation costs between the South-West and South-South. One foundational challenge to national growth has been the lack of continuity in government policies, including those that could have delivered long-term benefits if sustained. item.title: US offers $20m reward for info on ‘Iran’s nuclear program’: CENTCOM
item.description: Washington is offering a $20 million reward “and possible relocation” for information about Iran’s nuclear program, the US military said Friday, as President Donald Trump reiterated Tehran wants to make a deal to end the war. Read Also: Iran warns of wider war if US attacks after Trump election rout A State Department program, Rewards for Justice, “is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community,” US Central Command said on X. The program was established in 1984 under the State Department’s national security rewards program to offer money for information that protects American lives and interests. In its statement about the reward, the State Department said Iran’s “lack of compliance with the IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency) on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of ‘continuity of knowledge’ regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges. It gave no specific parameters on what information would yield a $20 million reward. Trump has repeatedly said US forces have effectively obliterated Iran’s nuclear program. “If we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today,” Trump said Friday night in West Palm Beach, Florida. “If they had nuclear, they would have used nuclear. They would have obliterated the Middle East.” But the president also said Iran – which he stressed has had its economy and military severely damaged over eight months of war – is eager to end the conflict. “We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly,” he said. Diplomatic efforts by mediators have been in full swing in an attempt to prevent any resumption of fighting. And on Tuesday Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his government was still trying to resolve the crisis through dialogue. Earlier this week Trump said he still had to “take care” of one or two targets, including so-called Pickaxe Mountain in central Iran, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. item.title: Trump: Lesson for Nigeria, by Stephanie Shaakaa
item.description: Donald Trump wanted the November 3 midterm elections to be about him. He said so repeatedly, urging Americans to vote as though his name were on the ballot. He wanted a Republican victory to demonstrate that his presidency still commanded popular support and that his influence over American politics remained firmly intact. Well, Americans took him seriously. Perhaps more seriously than he expected. Democrats have won control of both chambers of the United States Congress, delivering a major electoral setback to Trump and his Republican Party. Yet, as the results became clear, Trump reached for an explanation that seemed to contradict his own campaign message. In a post on his Truth Social platform, he declared: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” The irony is difficult to miss. He had spent weeks asking Americans to treat the election as a verdict on his presidency. When the verdict went against him, he suddenly appeared to be distancing himself from it. He wanted the political benefits of making the election about him without accepting the consequences when voters delivered an unfavourable answer. For readers in Nigeria, it is worth explaining what America calls midterm elections and why they matter. In the United States, a president is elected for a four-year term, but congressional elections take place every two years. This means that halfway into a president’s tenure, Americans return to the polls to elect members of the legislature. These elections are called midterms because they take place in the middle of a presidential term. Congress has two chambers: the House of Representatives and the Senate. All 435 seats in the House are contested every two years, while senators serve six-year terms, with approximately one-third of the 100 Senate seats contested every two years. Midterm elections do not determine who becomes president. The sitting president remains in office. Instead, voters decide which party controls Congress and, by extension, how much support or opposition the president will face in the legislature This gives Americans an opportunity to express satisfaction or dissatisfaction with a president’s performance without waiting another four years. They can strengthen the president’s party in Congress or hand control to the opposition, making it considerably more difficult for the president to advance his legislative agenda. That is precisely what has happened to Trump. American presidents often benefit from what is known as the coattail effect. When a president is popular, candidates from the same party can benefit from that popularity. His political strength becomes an advantage for others seeking elective office. But when a president becomes unpopular, the effect can work in reverse. Candidates associated with his administration may find themselves paying the price for public dissatisfaction with his leadership. item.title: From open pavilion to nation of orderlies: Is Zik’s ‘fear-free’ Nigeria still possible?
item.description: .What a 1960 inauguration says about fear in today’s corridors of power By Omeiza Ajayi Nearly 66 years after Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe was sworn in as Nigeria’s first African Governor-General, the footage of that day – which has again recently gone viral – raises an uncomfortable question: why did a leader who held the highest office in the land need no retinue of security details standing behind him, while today every minister, and even some local government supervisors, cannot move without a swarm of details? The inauguration took place on November 16, 1960, at Tafawa Balewa Square, barely six weeks after independence. It was also Zik’s 56th birthday. The narrator of the newsreel set the scene plainly. “At the steps of the pavilion stand the Prime Minister and the Lord Chief Justice, symbolising the people and the law, on what is surely one of the most important occasions in the history of the country.” No armed escort looms in the frame. No aide hovers at the shoulder of the man the crowd was chanting for. “Zik! Zik!” rang around the square as he arrived, and the vast stands, in the narrator’s words, were “hushed.” Today the picture is reversed. In Abuja and in the state capitals, orderlies trail ministers into halls and offices. The situation is so bad that some security personnel actually enter into very enclosed spaces or rooms with their AK47 rifles in clear breach of security protocol. At the local government level, some unelected supervisory councillors have been known to move with armed vigilance team members or hunters, sometimes to intimidate the very people they were appointed to serve. The easy explanation is insecurity, and it is not a false flag. Banditry, kidnapping and insurgency have made parts of the country dangerous, and no leader can be faulted for fearing for his life. But the leaders of other nations also face threats. Behind the American president or a British prime minister stand trained protective officers, assigned to a defined danger. They do not crowd every public official, from the cabinet room to the ward office, with men whose chief duty is to announce importance. It is not uncommon in Nigeria to see security details standing and blocking a television camera. That leaves the harder question. Are Nigeria’s leaders afraid of the general state of the country, or have they become afraid of their own people? Zik, standing in the open that November morning, appeared to have settled that question for himself. He began his address with these words: “It is with humility, mingled with joy, that I thank this grand concourse of patriots and friends of Nigeria for congregating here today on the occasion of my inauguration as the first African Governor General and Commander-in-Chief of the Federation of Nigeria.” He titled the speech “Respect for Human Dignity,” and he made no secret of what he feared for Nigeria. item.title: Daddy Showkey: Vanguard Award will be the biggest of my lifetime
item.description: By Clifford Ndujihe & Benjamin Njoku Chief John Odafe Asiemo, 57, popularly known as Daddy Showkey, is a household name in Nigerian music scene. He is the creator of ‘Galala’ music, which sound helped define Nigeria’s street music in the 90s. Read Also: Nostalgia, glitz as icons reunite for Daddy Showkey’s 50th anniversary celebration Daddy Showkey is a nominee for Vanguard Newspaper’s 2026 Entertainment Icon of the year award. Speaking with ululation after being presented with the letter of nomination, on Tuesday at his Lagos residence, he said: “They say a prophet is not recognised by his own people. But I am a prophet who is being recognised by the people who built me. This is the greatest awards I have ever received in my life because it is coming from Vanguard. Vanguard is the first newspaper in Nigeria that wrote about me, when I was nothing. This is Vanguard, and I cherish it a lot. “Apart from that, Vanguard played a big role in pushing me to the limelight. “So, a recognition award coming from Vanguard, I must cherish it. It is like my own people saying it is high time. Sometimes, when I see Vanguard giving people awards, I always say in my mind, when is it going to be my turn? “Now, it is my turn to receive the award and I am very grateful.” Reminiscing on his early days, Daddy Showkey, who celebrated 50 years on the stage recently, continued: “For years, I kept coming to Vanguard head office, but I never met the publisher, Uncle Sam, in person. After my secondary education, I hit the streets. From childhood, I had made up my mind to follow music. At 13, in 1983, I started following Danladi Bako of NTA. I was always at his office on Lagos Island. He would give me a voucher to go and eat, and made me comfortable in his office. My first song, “Big Belle”, was released in 1990 in Nawfia, Njikoka, Enugu-Ukwu, Anambra State. I cannot forget the late Amadi Ogbonna(former Vanguard Entertainment Editor). He was one of the earliest journalists to write about me and played a huge role in my career. Before Ogbonnaya wrote about me, we used to walk from Kirikiri to Olodi areas, passing Vanguard. I remember saying one day while walking past Vanguard ‘this newspaper will one day write about me.’ It came to pass when Ogbonnaya wrote about me for the first time. The second was Smart Irewudo, a former Champion Newspaper reporter, now based in the United States. Before I started recording, during the June 12 crisis, I led Ajegunle boys who blocked roads and extorted money from motorists. Smart took my picture and published it in the Daily Champion. In his mind, he thought he had done me a great favour. He didn’t know the police would come after me. Luckily, one of the policemen from Area F showed my picture to Amadi Ogbonna. He recognised me immediately and called me. When I showed up, Ogbonna took me to the police station and told them I wasn’t a bad boy, they should release me and focus on arresting real criminals. item.title: Police rescue 10 stolen children in Abia
item.description: By Steve Oko UMUAHIA—The Abia State Police Command has arrested suspects linked to the October 17 attack on Uratta Divisional Police Headquarters, rescued 10 stolen children and recovered 15 firearms and 30 stolen vehicles in a major security crackdown across the state. The Command also disclosed that it arrested 109 suspects, comprising 89 males and 20 females, in connection with 211 criminal cases recorded between September 11, 2026 and November 6, 2026. Commissioner of Police, CP Wilfred Afolabi, who disclosed this on Friday while presenting the Command’s operational scorecard, said the arrests followed intelligence-driven operations and collaboration with other security agencies. On the Uratta police station attack, Afolabi said investigations had led to the arrest of some of the suspected attackers, with one of them allegedly confessing to leading the gang that carried out the assault. He said investigations were ongoing to track down other accomplices and establish the full circumstances surrounding the attack. In a related security operation, operatives of the Anti-Kidnapping Unit raided a location at Ubakala, Umuahia South Local Government Area, on October 25, arresting a suspect identified as Osita. The police reportedly recovered two locally fabricated guns, 16 live cartridges and four expended cartridges from the suspect. Another suspect, 30-year-old suspect, was subsequently arrested for allegedly supplying ammunition illegally. Both suspects have been charged to court, according to the CP. On child trafficking, Afolabi said police operatives rescued 10 children during the period under review and reunited them with their families. He specifically disclosed that two suspects, including a 38-year-old , were arrested on October 11 over the alleged stealing of two children, seven-year-old Chiamaka Chikeze and nine-month-old Goodluck Chikeze. The children were reportedly recovered and handed back to their parents, while the suspects were charged to court. The police boss also announced the arrest of a five-man vehicle theft syndicate, aged 43, and 40. A Toyota Corolla with registration number ROU 9338J was recovered from the suspects, who have also been charged to court. In another operation, two suspected cultists, aged 27, and 25, were arrested on October 31 for allegedly dispossessing students of Abia State University, Uturu, of their mobile phones and other valuables at gunpoint. A locally fabricated firearm was recovered from them. The CP said one of the suspects had confessed to belonging to the Black Axe Confraternity, adding that efforts were ongoing to apprehend other members of the gang. item.title: ‘Sort out your internal mess’, APC tells Atiku, ADC after court judgment
item.description: By Omeiza Ajayi The All Progressives Congress APC has told the Senator David Mark-led faction of the African Democratic Congress ADC to go sort out its internal mess and quit its “senseless rants” after a Federal High Court judgment sacked the faction’s leadership. Read Also: ADC Crisis: What becomes of Atiku, Mark, Gombe if Supreme Court decides party’s fate? In a statement Friday in Abuja, the APC National Publicity Secretary, Felix Morka, said the ruling party had no hand in the case. “To be clear, APC is neither a party nor an interlocutor in the matter. Nothing about the case has anything to do with the APC. And the APC has absolutely no role in the party’s judicial quagmire,” he said. The judgment, delivered on Thursday by Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja, sacked the David Mark-led leadership of the ADC. It also nullified all official acts of that leadership, including its primary election processes and outcomes, like the presidential candidacy of former vice president Atiku Abubakar. Morka said the case was brought by ADC national officers against the faction now removed from office, describing the suit as “a notorious case initiated by leaders of ADC against pirate leaders of ADC.” He accused Mark and his associates of taking over the party “to satisfy Atiku Abubakar’s quixotic presidential ambition.” According to him, “it didn’t matter to them that their hostile takeover of that party was in flagrant violation of the rule of law and ADC’s internal democracy, as a court of competent jurisdiction has now declared.” The APC spokesman also accused the ADC of reacting to court decisions according to whether they favour it. “Every time a court decides against the Senator David Mark-led factional African Democratic Congress, they accuse the All Progressives Congress of collusion and deprecate the judiciary. Every time a court decides in their favour, they hail the rule of law and extol the judiciary,” he said. He added that the faction’s attitude showed “no iota of regard for the authority and independence of the judiciary, an indispensable pillar of any democracy.” On Thursday’s ruling, Morka said it “was procured by their own lawlessness and demonstrates the vibrancy of the rule of law and independence of the judiciary in Nigeria.” He said the ADC leaders “take no responsibility or accountability for the self-inflicted injury that the court only judicially certified.” Vanguard News The post ‘Sort out your internal mess’, APC tells Atiku, ADC after court judgment appeared first on Vanguard News .

item.title: Scientists turn cancer cells into weapons against tumours
item.description: By Sola Ogundipe What if the chemical produced in abundance by cancer cells could be turned against the cancers? What if, instead of flooding the entire body with powerful drugs in an attempt to destroy a tumour, scientists could persuade cancer cells to manufacture destructive chemicals from within? That possibility is at the centre of an intriguing scientific breakthrough in Japan, where researchers have developed an experimental technique that exploits carbon monoxide produced by cancer cells to generate cancer-killing compounds inside them. The approach turns an unusual feature of cancer biology into a potential therapeutic advantage. Rather than administering an already manufactured toxic drug that circulates through the body and can damage healthy tissues, the researchers have devised a chemical system that produces an anticancer compound inside targeted cancer cells. In laboratory experiments, the technique successfully generated toxic compounds in several cancer cell lines while leaving a noncancerous cell line without detectable production of the same compound. Although still at an early experimental stage, the findings could open a new direction in cancer treatment, particularly in the long-standing search for ways to destroy malignant cells while sparing healthy tissues from the collateral damage associated with conventional chemotherapy. The research, led by Katsunori Tanaka at the RIKEN Pioneering Research Institute (PRI), Japan, was published in Nature Communications. Cancer treatment has long been complicated by a fundamental problem: drugs powerful enough to destroy malignant cells can also injure normal cells. Chemotherapy, for instance, often affects healthy tissues because many anticancer medicines cannot distinguish perfectly between cancerous and noncancerous cells. The resulting damage can produce debilitating side effects, including nausea, fatigue, hair loss and suppression of the immune system. Scientists have consequently been exploring more selective ways of delivering or generating anticancer agents at the precise location where they are needed. Tanaka and colleagues focused on carbon monoxide, a gas commonly recognised for its toxicity but also naturally produced in small quantities in the human body. Their strategy was to deliver a metal-based catalyst into cells and use the available carbon monoxide as the chemical fuel for a reaction that manufactures an anticancer substance. In principle, the reaction would be activated predominantly in cancer cells, where sufficient carbon monoxide is available, rather than in healthy tissues. The research represents part of a developing scientific field known as therapeutic in vivo synthetic chemistry, which seeks to use chemical reactions inside living organisms to manufacture therapeutic substances where they are needed. item.title: Nigeria is losing $1.6bn yearly to avoidable blindness — Aghaji
item.description: By Prisca Sam-Duru Almost on a daily basis, across Nigeria and much of Africa, millions of people wake up to a world they cannot see clearly. A farmer peeks at his cassava farms for instance, but cannot differentiate the difference between weed and crop. A trader holds her register at arm’s length, guessing at figures she once read at a glance. A child in the back row of a classroom copies from a board that is almost a blur. More often, an old woman needs her grandchild to lead her to the market because the road she walked for over 50 years has become unrecognizable. Those are not statistics. They are the human face of a crisis that Africa has lived with for too long. As Professor Ada Aghaji told a packed hall at the University of Nigeria on October 29, 2026, this is a crisis Africa can no longer afford to ignore. Delivering the institution’s 254th Inaugural Lecture, titled “Let There Be Sight: Building Sustainable Eye Health Systems for All in Africa,” Aghaji, Professor of Ophthalmology and Eye Health Systems, made a simple but very powerful argument: eye health in Africa is not just a medical issue. It is an economic issue. A development issue. A justice issue. And the numbers prove it. According to her, Nigeria loses an estimated $1.6 billion every year in productivity because of vision impairment. Across Africa, the loss is about $9 billion. Globally, it stands at a staggering $410 billion. Behind those figures are livelihoods cut short, schooling interrupted, and families pushed deeper into poverty. Yet, as Aghaji stressed, much of this vision loss can be prevented or treated. A pair of spectacles costing less than a bag of rice. A 15-minute cataract operation. A routine screening at a primary health centre. Why, then, do millions of Africans continue to live with avoidable blindness when the solutions already exist? That was the question at the heart of her lecture. Two Children, Two Worlds Perhaps the most haunting moment of the lecture came not from statistics, but from a story. Aghaji spoke of two children born with congenital rubella syndrome; a condition that can cause cataracts, deafness and other disabilities. One was born in Nigeria. He faced delays, barriers to treatment and rehabilitation, and ended up blind. The other was a Somali refugee child in England. He received timely surgery, spectacles and hearing aids, and with them, a chance to learn, to play, to grow Their medical conditions were similar. Their opportunities were profoundly different. The contrast, Aghaji argued, is the story of Africa’s eye health system in miniature. Medical knowledge alone does not guarantee care. What determines whether a child sees or goes blind is often not the disease, but the system around it: whether there is money to pay, a health worker to detect the problem, a referral that works, a hospital that can be reached. item.title: Naira would’ve been worthless, moved with wheelbarrow if we didn’t act – Tinubu
item.description: President Bola Tinubu said that Naira would have been so worthless, it would be moved about by wheelbarrow if not for his economic policies that moved Nigeria away from the brink of financial collapse. He described the January 16, 2027 election as consequential, saying it would determine the country’s direction. Defending his economic policies, Tinubu said his administration had moved Nigeria away from the brink of financial collapse. According to him, “This coming election, on January 16th is a consequential election. It will define the direction of this country. “When I took over, 27 governors out of 36 of this country were unable to pay salary, not to talk of pension, and gratuity. Today, I can say that we are out of that tunnel. “And I can beat my chest to say we are out of the despair, the dark tunnel of uncertainty and the calamity of a possible bankruptcy. “By now if we didn’t take over, if we didn’t do what we did, we will be using the wheelbarrows to move our naira about because it will have become valueless.” On young voters The President urged the electorate, particularly young people, to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards, PVCs. item.title: ADC Crisis: What becomes of Atiku, Mark, Gombe if Supreme Court decides party’s fate?
item.description: By Luminous Jannamike The African Democratic Congress (ADC) was meant to be the meeting point of opposition forces determined to challenge President Bola Tinubu in 2027. Instead, the party has become the battleground for a struggle that could undo the coalition it was expected to accommodate. Read Also: Court sacks Mark-led ADC exco, voids Atiku’s candidacy Barely 24 hours after former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar took his presidential campaign to Sokoto, a Federal High Court judgment delivered by Justice Peter Lifu threw the party into fresh uncertainty, nullifying the David Mark-led leadership and decisions taken under it, including the process that produced Atiku as presidential candidate. For Mark and his allies, it was a setback at a critical moment. For Nafiu Bala Gombe, who challenged the leadership transition, it was a victory in a battle he had refused to abandon. For Atiku, it was a reminder that the platform on which he hopes to return to Aso Rock may not be entirely within his control. With the Mark faction preparing to appeal, attention is shifting to the appellate courts. Whatever the eventual outcome, the political fortunes of some of the coalition’s most prominent figures are at stake. How it all began The dispute began when former ADC National Chairman, Ralph Nwosu, facilitated a leadership transition that brought Mark and former Osun State Governor, Rauf Aregbesola, into the party as National Chairman and National Secretary respectively. The arrangement offered opposition politicians an existing political structure around which to build a challenge to the APC. But Gombe, a former Deputy National Chairman, North, objected, arguing that the party’s constitution provided a succession procedure that was not followed. His challenge produced Justice Lifu’s November 5 judgment. The Mark faction, however, insists that the leadership question had already been examined by the court. It points to the July 2, 2026, judgment of Justice Musa Liman in a separate suit instituted by House of Representatives member Leke Abejide. Justice Liman upheld preliminary objections, including lack of jurisdiction, standing and failure to exhaust internal party remedies. He also made findings favourable to the defendants concerning the leadership transition The Mark camp argues that a court of coordinate jurisdiction cannot overturn another court’s decision. However, the different plaintiffs and the precise issues and reliefs sought in the two cases make the legal relationship between the judgments a matter requiring highest judicial determination. The Supreme Court had intervened on April 30, setting aside an earlier status quo ante bellum order and directing an expedited hearing at the Federal High Court. item.title: CBN updates guidelines for stablecoins operation
item.description: •Sets N15bn capital requirement By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The Central Bank of Nigeria has issued guidelines for virtual asset providers in the country, setting minimum capital requirement of N10 billion and N15 billion for Classes 1 and 2 issuers, respectively. This was contained in a circular with reference number PSP/DIR/PUB/CIR/001/004, date November 5, 2026 and signed by the Director of Payments Systems Policy, Mr. Musa Jimoh. According to the bank, “A Class 1 Licensed Issuer shall maintain paid-up capital of N10 billion Naira or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter. Class 2 Licensed Issuer shall maintain minimum paid-up capital of N15 billion or such higher amount as the Bank may prescribe, on entry and at all times thereafter. “Both classes shall comply with the capital deposit and corresponding evidence and supplementary requirements in Section 17. There is no offshore issuer exemption from incorporation, licensing or capital.” Class 2 stablecoins are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value against foreign currencies, including the US dollar, while Class 1 refers to issuers of naira-referenced stablecoins. CBN said the emergence of virtual assets, stablecoins, and tokenised payment instruments “presents significant opportunities for innovation in payments, remittances, settlement, and digital commerce,” but that, “their growing adoption also introduces risks relating to financial stability, monetary policy, consumer protection, illicit finance, operational resilience, and foreign exchange management.” It added that the guidelines were issued pursuant to its statutory mandate to promote monetary and financial stability and regulate Nigeria’s payments system. “These Guidelines establish a risk-based framework for the licensing, regulation, supervision, and oversight of Non-Security Virtual Assets, including stablecoins, Deposit Money Tokens (DMTs), and related Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs). “These Guidelines seek to support responsible innovation while safeguarding the integrity, stability, and efficiency of the Nigerian financial system. “These Guidelines also seek to provide regulatory requirements relating to governance, prudential standards, consumer protection, operational resilience, AML/CFT/CPF compliance, and reporting obligations for entities and persons engaged in regulated non-security virtual asset activities within or involving Nigeria,” the bank explained. The CBN’s updated framework outlines clear boundaries for Virtual Asset Service Providers (VASPs), with a sharp focus on foreign exchange liquidity, consumer protection, and peer-to-peer (P2P) trading identity protocols. Curbing money laundering The guidelines place great responsibilities on issuers to ensure that their activities do not aid money laundering or terrorism financing, as they are required to provide detailed data on their customers. item.title: January 2027: Tinubu’s achilles heel, by Muyiwa Adetiba
item.description: The world witnessed a blue wave as the Democrats swept the recently concluded mid-term elections in the United States. Many contested areas had a touch of blue. Even areas that had always been crimson turned deep purple as Democrats made significant inroads into republican comfort zones. Many Republican Congressmen ended up winning in these areas by the skin of their teeth. It was the worse rout in years, some say decades. To be fair, the signs were always there that Republicans would drop seats. Incumbents always do traditionally. And this incumbent had done little to sway tradition. If anything, he exacerbated it. Affordability was an issue in the US – as it still is in many parts of the world – before President Trump ascended the most powerful seat in the world. It was, along immigration, one of the things he promised to tackle. Instead, he toyed with it, calling it fake and a ruse for Democrats to gain attention. But affordability was a reality that stared an average American in the face every time they visited the stores. It was neither red nor blue. The negative rating at the polls for the President showed they were not amused. Something needed to be done to stem the poor rating when the mid-term elections were less than a year away. So the man who loves to be loved, the deal maker who loves quick fixes, the closet dictator who loves a show of power invaded Iran and killed – for want of a milder word – all their leaders in one fell swoop. He rode roughshod into a territory his predecessors had feared to tread. He thought it would all be over in weeks and his rating would get a lift. He thought he would emerge as a knight in shining armor – Americans love a war hero. But Iran is no Venezuela. This ill-advised war of choice is in its ninth month with no end in sight. Only casualties. Only consequences. One of the consequences is the cost of fuel. And by the time he embarked on his frenzied campaign tour to try to stave the threatening blue wave, it was too little, too late. Besides, he was seen as the problem by many and it is not often that the problem becomes the solution. The Iran war has destabilized the Middle-East which is the world’s energy belt. The consequence of that has reverberated all over the world and has become a tipping point to countries which are already contending with affordability issues. The recent riots in Europe and Latin America are examples of discontents caused by a rising cost of living. The result of the recent mid-term election in the US is, in many ways, a consequence of that as well. It is a bad time to seek a re-election as the Israeli Prime Minister and many world leaders have found out. Nigeria goes to the poll in just about two months. item.title: Supreme Court Justices placed on US visa ban – Retiring jurist
item.description: •Judgement that gave Uzodimma governorship victory fingered By Ikechukwu Nnochiri A retiring Justice of the Supreme Court, Justice Uwani Abba-Aji, disclosed on Friday that some justices of the court had been placed on a visa ban by the United States of America. Read Also : Uzodinma sworn-in as sixth governor of Imo Justice Abba-Aji, speaking during a valedictory session held to mark her retirement from the bench, said the travel ban followed a judgment of the apex court that she described as widely misinterpreted. She said: “My time on the Supreme Court bench was filled with challenges, some of which have served as additional opportunities to stand firm on the side of justice, regardless of the consequences. “One of such challenging judgments was widely misinterpreted and led to a travel ban to the United States of America being imposed on all members of the panel, a ban which still holds today.” Even though Justice Abba-Aji did not mention the specific case that led to the imposition of a US visa ban on Supreme Court Justices, Vanguard understands that it was connected to the legal tussle that followed the 2019 governorship election in Imo State. A seven-member panel of the Supreme Court, which included the current Chief Justice of Nigeria (CJN), Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, and Justice Abba-Aji, had on January 14, 2020, nullified the election of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate, Emeka Ihedioha, and ordered the swearing-in of the candidate of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Senator Hope Uzodimma, who had initially finished fourth in the governorship election. In the lead judgment delivered by the CJN, the apex court ordered the immediate withdrawal of the Certificate of Return that had already been issued to Ihedioha by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). It ordered that a fresh Certificate of Return be issued to Uzodimma as the validly elected governor of Imo State. To arrive at the decision, the apex court panel vacated the concurrent verdicts of both the Court of Appeal and the Imo State Governorship Election Petitions Tribunal, which had earlier affirmed the PDP candidate as winner of the gubernatorial contest. Votes counted in courtroom The panel went ahead to add election results from 388 polling units, amounting to 213,295 votes, which were tendered before the tribunal by a police officer who testified as PW-54, but which INEC disowned. After all the votes were computed inside the courtroom, Uzodimma was declared the candidate who secured the majority of lawful votes cast at the election, a judgment that elicited wide reactions and protests. Other members of the panel, which was led by the then CJN, Justice Tanko Muhammad, were Justices Sylvester Ngwuta, Kayode Ariwola and Amiru Sanusi. Although Ihedioha subsequently approached the apex court again for a review of the judgment, which he insisted occasioned a miscarriage of justice, his application was refused. item.title: Mutfwang: Educated Nigerians masterminding corruption, institutional decay
item.description: …says professionals behind major governance failures …challenges graduates to choose integrity over wealth By Joseph Erunke, Abuja Plateau State Governor, Caleb Mutfwang, has accused educated Nigerians of masterminding some of the country’s most damaging corruption scandals, financial fraud and institutional abuses, saying the nation’s governance crisis is not a result of a shortage of intellectual capacity but a failure of conscience. Mutfwang said some of the most sophisticated acts of financial fraud, contract manipulation, money laundering and subversion of public institutions were perpetrated by people whose academic qualifications and professional expertise should ordinarily be deployed for national development. The governor spoke on Friday in Abuja while delivering the convocation lecture at the 15th Convocation Ceremony of Veritas University. In his lecture titled, “Building the Nigeria We Want: The Role of the Educated Mind,” he warned that education without moral discipline had become a dangerous instrument against the country’s progress. He challenged the graduating students to rethink the purpose of university education, insisting that academic certificates and intellectual brilliance would amount to little if deployed for selfish interests at the expense of society. According to him, Nigeria’s development challenges cannot be blamed entirely on inadequate manpower or lack of expertise, as many individuals responsible for undermining public institutions are highly educated and professionally trained. Describing the situation as an uncomfortable reality the country must confront, Mutfwang said some of Nigeria’s most entrenched governance failures were products of educated minds. He said: “Indeed, I make an uncomfortable observation: the afflictions I diagnosed earlier, prebendalism, the privatisation of public office, grand corruption, the capture of institutions, are almost never the work of illiterate minds. They are overwhelmingly executed by educated minds. “The contract, the doctored account, the laundered fund, the ingenious evasion of law. All these are the signatures of trained minds. This is the paradox we must confront. The educated mind is at once our greatest hope, and when corrupted, it becomes our most sophisticated danger.” The governor also cited internet fraudsters, popularly known as Yahoo boys, as an example of intelligence deployed in the wrong direction, arguing that criminal ingenuity reflected a lack of moral restraint rather than an absence of intelligence. “The Yahoo boy is certainly not a derelict. He is a work of intelligence, but intelligence wrongly applied,” he said. Mutfwang maintained that Nigeria had no shortage of brilliant citizens, noting the achievements of Nigerians across different professions and on international platforms. However, he lamented that the country had failed to translate its abundant intellectual resources into responsible leadership, accountable governance and sustainable developme

item.title: 2027: APGA adopts Tinubu, flags off nationwide campaign
item.description: …Soludo cites South-East projects, urges strategic voting By Steve Oko The All Progressives Grand Alliance (APGA) has adopted President Bola Tinubu as its presidential candidate for the 2027 general election, with Anambra State Governor, Prof. Chukwuma Soludo, saying the decision was informed by the need for progressive forces to work together. Soludo made the declaration on Friday while flagging off APGA’s nationwide election campaign at Alex Ekwueme Square, Awka, Anambra State, where the party unveiled more than 253 candidates contesting various elective positions across the country. The governor, who is APGA’s National Leader, said the decision to support Tinubu was consistent with the party’s political tradition, recalling that APGA had similarly adopted former President Goodluck Jonathan in the 2011 and 2015 presidential elections. He said the party’s support for Tinubu was also informed by what he described as the Federal Government’s commitment to the South-East, particularly in infrastructure development. “Today, as we unveil our campaign as the foremost progressive party in Nigeria, we are also officially adopting President Bola Tinubu as the presidential candidate of APGA. “We did it in 2011 and 2015 for President Jonathan. We are repeating it in 2027 because progressives are working together to support a President who loves Ndi Igbo and Ndi Anambra,” Soludo declared. Citing the dualisation and rehabilitation of the Enugu-Onitsha Expressway and other federal projects in the region, the governor urged voters to approach the 2027 elections with political pragmatism rather than sentiment. He said voting decisions should be guided by tangible benefits, enlightened self-interest and strategic political considerations capable of advancing the interests of the South-East. Soludo also charged APGA candidates and members to intensify grassroots mobilisation through door-to-door campaigns, assuring them that he would personally join the candidates in soliciting votes. He expressed confidence in the party’s electoral prospects, urging voters to distinguish between reason and emotion ahead of the January 16 and February 6, 2027 elections. At the event, Soludo presented party flags to 44 APGA candidates contesting legislative seats in Anambra State. The candidates comprised three senatorial candidates, 11 House of Representatives candidates and 30 State House of Assembly candidates. Earlier, APGA National Chairman, Barrister Sly Ezeokenwa, commended Soludo for what he described as transparent and competitive party primaries conducted in compliance with electoral laws. Ezeokenwa attributed the influx of new members into the party to Soludo’s people-oriented policies, describing Anambra as APGA’s political stronghold. He expressed confidence that the party would record a decisive victory in the forthcoming elections. item.title: Ebonyi Youths Protest Political Violence, Intimidation Ahead Of 2027 Elections
item.description: Hundreds of youths in Ebonyi State have staged a peaceful march through Abakaliki, the state capital, calling for an end to political violence, intimidation and harassment of opposition members ahead of the 2027 general elections. The protesters, under the aegis of Concerned Ebonyi Youth for Democracy, said they came from the 13 local government areas of the state to demand a peaceful political atmosphere in which all citizens can participate without fear. The demonstrators marched through major streets in Abakaliki, displaying placards with messages including, “Democracy Needs Peaceful Ideas, Not Weapons” and “Protect Freedom of Speech in Ebonyi.” Addressing journalists during the rally, a spokesperson for the group said the youths would not accept any attempt to undermine their constitutional rights. “Our constitutional rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly are not negotiable,” the spokesperson said. The group also expressed concern over reported incidents of physical violence, harassment and voter intimidation targeting opposition figures in parts of the state. “We will not sit by while political thuggery and intimidation threaten to ruin our state’s democratic process. Every citizen, regardless of party alignment, deserves to participate without fear for their safety,” the spokesperson added. The protesters called on security agencies and state institutions to intervene and ensure a level playing field for all political parties. Another youth coordinator said opposition parties should be able to campaign, present their programmes and engage voters without threats or intimidation. “Opposition parties must be allowed to campaign safely, present their platforms, and engage with voters without constant threat of violence,” the coordinator said. The group said the march was part of efforts by young people in the state to demand accountability and promote peaceful political participation as the 2027 general elections approach. item.title: ‘It’ll Never Be Forgotten’, Flamingos Captain On Hopes Of Winning U-17 World Cup
item.description: Nigeria’s U-17 women’s team captain, Harmony Chidi, says winning the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup would be an unforgettable moment for her, her teammates, the coaching crew and the country. Speaking to FIFA ahead of the final against Japan in Morocco, Chidi described reaching the last stage of the competition as a significant achievement but said lifting the trophy would make the occasion even more special. “I think it would be a great thing, a joy, and would never be forgotten in life,” she said. “Reaching the final is a very big thing, it’s a great thing and it’s something that we have dreamed of. Winning would be something myself, my country, my team-mates, our coaches, and everybody would be proud of.” The Flamingos have made history by becoming the first African team to reach the final of the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, setting up a title clash with Japan. Their journey to the final followed a difficult start, having lost 2-1 to Poland in their opening Group B match. They recovered to win five consecutive games against Puerto Rico, two-time reigning champions DPR Korea, Mexico, Venezuela and Brazil. Their 3-1 victory over Brazil in the semi-final secured their place in the final and kept alive Nigeria’s hopes of winning the competition for the first time. Head coach Akeem Busari said the team’s response to the opening defeat was driven by psychological guidance, renewed confidence and a change in the players’ attitude and approach. Flamingos captain Chidi Harmony and coach Akeem Busari in a photoshoot with the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup trophy ahead of the final against Japan. Photo credit: fifa.com “After the first game, we needed to sit them down, psychologically talk to them, talk about our game plan and all we have been doing in the sessions,” he told FIFA. “We needed to change our attitude and character, but because of their age, we just needed to talk to them, to counsel them, and those are the points that make the difference.” Busari acknowledged Japan’s quality, pointing to what he observed in their match against DPR Korea, but said the final would present a different challenge for both teams. “From what we saw against DPR Korea, I think it’s the core of what we should expect more of from the Japanese,” he said. “But it’s a different ballgame because, for both us and them, the game will not be the same. The character, mentality and attitude which you approach every game with, and at every other level too, is what really matters.” The coach, who had declared before the tournament that Nigeria wanted to become champions, credited the players for the team’s progress, describing them as the people who had made the achievement possible. “It would be a plus for Africa, for Nigeria, for my own career as a person, but also for the players as well – they are the gladiators. Without them, we could not do anything,” he said. With the final within reach, Busari said the players must remain focused and understand that their work was not over sim

item.title: The Obidient Pulse: Obi Warns Against Uncertainty As Opposition Groups Face A Test Of Unity
item.description: A court ruling that has thrown the African Democratic Congress into fresh uncertainty has prompted Peter Obi to warn about the consequences for opposition politics, while disagreements continue among groups supporting his own 2027 bid. Obi reacts to court ruling affecting ADC The Federal High Court in Abuja has nullified the leadership of the African Democratic Congress under Senator David Mark and set aside the party’s processes, including the nomination of Atiku Abubakar as its presidential candidate. The ADC says it will appeal. Obi, the Nigeria Democratic Congress presidential candidate, described the ruling as “unsettling and surprising”. He said there should be certainty about parties and candidates ahead of an election and called for opposition politics to be protected. Obi also accused the ruling APC of engineering the instability, an allegation the party rejected. The court decision concerns the ADC; it does not directly affect Obi’s NDC candidacy. Court fight places opposition unity under pressure The ADC has rejected the judgment and says it will challenge it in court. Atiku has also said he will appeal and seek a stay of execution. The case now puts the spotlight on the judiciary’s role in resolving internal party disputes and on whether opposition parties can maintain stable platforms as the election approaches. Disagreement among Obi’s support groups continues The court ruling comes amid public friction between the OK Movement and leaders of the Obidient Movement and NDC campaign. The OK Movement accused them of fuelling divisions; the NDC campaign dismissed the dispute as a distraction, while the Obidient coordinator’s aide said he was focused on mobilising support for Obi. The exchanges raise a practical question for the campaign: can its different support groups coordinate their work, clarify who speaks for whom and build lasting grassroots organisation? The public disagreements are a reminder that a broad support base needs clear roles and disciplined coordination to turn enthusiasm into effective political mobilisation. The task ahead For the Obidient Movement, the immediate challenge is to keep attention on voters, organisation and the issues facing Nigerians. The movement’s strength will be measured not only by the size of its support, but by how effectively it organises that support across communities and sustains a credible campaign. In a political season increasingly shaped by court cases and internal disputes, the demand from supporters is likely to be simple: less public quarrelling, clearer communication and visible work on the ground.
